notes: Duvalier's National Unity Party (PUN) holds ruling slot 13 with the MD PUN sprite. Tonton Macoutes (VSN) in 21, Presidential Guard in 7, army FAd'H in 22 (MD sprite). PUCH (1969 merger) in 4, Fignolé's MOP in 18, Déjoie's PAIN in 1, Magloire exiles in 0, Catholic hierarchy in 14, Les Griots (noirisme) in 20.

0.name: Les Magloiristes
0.text:
The Magloirists are the followers of General Paul Magloire, president from 1950 to 1956, whose era of tourism, public works and close friendship with Washington ended in a general strike. Living in exile in New York, Magloire remains a figurehead for officers, businessmen and politicians driven out by Duvalier.

They promise a return to order without terror: an army restored as guardian of the state, a cooperative relationship with the United States, foreign investment and protection of the elite. Their supporters are exiled officers, the old mulatto bourgeoisie and conservative Catholics. Their leverage lies in American contacts and exile money.

1.name: Parti Agricole et Industriel National
1.text:
The National Agricultural and Industrial Party was founded by the senator and agronomist Louis Déjoie, a wealthy planter and industrialist, for the 1957 presidential election he lost to François Duvalier amid fraud and violence. Déjoie fled into exile, from where he has backed plots against the regime; the party survives only in exile networks and among discreet sympathizers at home.

The PAIN stands for private enterprise, modern agriculture, honest administration and close ties with the United States. Its base is the commercial and landowning elite, much of it mulatto, the southern towns and the professions. Its leverage lies in money, connections abroad and hopes of a post-Duvalier transition.

2.name: Les Exilés de Montréal
2.text:
The Exiles of Montreal are Haitian doctors, teachers, lawyers and writers who fled Duvalier's terror in the 1960s and settled in Quebec, where they publish bulletins, organize forums and lobby the Canadian government. Similar circles exist in New York and Paris, linked by émigré newspapers and church networks.

They demand civil liberties, free elections, an independent judiciary, amnesty for political prisoners and the disbanding of the Tonton Macoutes, and look to North American liberal democracy as a model. Their influence lies in education, the press and the growing remittances of the diaspora rather than in any following at home.

3.name: Jeunesse Ouvrière Chrétienne
3.text:
The Young Christian Workers, the Catholic workers' youth movement founded in Belgium by Joseph Cardijn, built Haitian sections among urban workers and rural youth. Duvalier's war on the Church in the early 1960s, with the expulsion of bishops, foreign priests and the Jesuits, drove many of its chaplains and leaders abroad or underground.

Following Cardijn's method of see, judge, act, it promotes trade unions, cooperatives, literacy and social justice for workers and peasants, rejecting both Duvalierist terror and communism. Its leverage lies in parish networks, Catholic schools and the solidarity of Christian labour movements abroad.

4.name: Parti Unifié des Communistes Haïtiens
4.text:
The Unified Party of Haitian Communists was formed in January 1969 by merging the People's Entente Party, founded by the novelist Jacques Stephen Alexis, and the People's Party of National Liberation. Within months the regime destroyed its armed wing: fighters were killed in Port-au-Prince and peasants of Cazale massacred for sheltering them. Surviving leaders such as Gérard Pierre-Charles and René Théodore operate from exile.

The PUCH follows the pro-Soviet line of a national-democratic, anti-imperialist and anti-feudal revolution against Duvalier and American domination. Its base is students, intellectuals and urban workers. Decimated at home, it relies on exile networks in Mexico, Moscow and Eastern Europe.

5.name: Kamoken
5.text:
Kamoken is the Creole name given to the armed anti-Duvalier exiles who landed in Haiti in 1964, among them Fred Baptiste's guerrillas in the southeast and the Jeune Haïti band in the Grand'Anse, all hunted down by the army and the militia. Survivors and younger admirers in the Dominican Republic, New York and Caracas still dream of a new landing.

The Kamoken believe only armed struggle can bring down the dictatorship and open the way to social revolution, drawing on Cuban foquismo and Haitian traditions of peasant resistance. Their base is radical exile youth and a few rural sympathizers. Their leverage lies in daring, not numbers.

6.name: Bizango
6.text:
The Bizango are the secret societies of rural Vodou, with their own emperors, presidents and night-time processions, that have long enforced customary justice in the countryside. Duvalier, a former ethnologist, has drawn many oungan and society leaders into the Tonton Macoutes and the network of rural section chiefs, binding folk religion to the state.

As a political bloc they stand for an African-rooted Haitian identity against the Catholic, mulatto and Western establishment, distrust foreign missionaries and modernizers, and defend the peasant moral order. Their power lies in fear, ritual authority and control of the night in the countryside.

7.name: Garde Présidentielle
7.text:
The Presidential Guard is the elite unit quartered in and beside the National Palace in Port-au-Prince, built up by Duvalier as a counterweight to the regular army after repeated coup plots. It controls the capital's heaviest weapons, and its officers are chosen for personal loyalty to the president.

As a power bloc it embodies rule by the security apparatus: suspicion of foreigners, including American diplomats blamed for past plots, preventive repression and the survival of the Duvalier family above all. It eyes the Tonton Macoutes as rivals for the president's trust. Its leverage lies in its place at the centre of power when the ailing president's succession arrives.

8.name: Les Amis de Tyr
8.text:
The Friends of Tyre are a few Shia families from southern Lebanon within Haiti's Levantine merchant colony, which is otherwise overwhelmingly Christian. They keep shops on the Grand-Rue of Port-au-Prince and in Cap-Haïtien and follow the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who in 1969 became head of Lebanon's Supreme Islamic Shia Council.

They seek dignity and mutual aid for their community, education for their children and peaceful coexistence with Catholics and Vodou practitioners, staying clear of politics under a regime that eyes the Syrian traders with suspicion. Their influence is limited to commerce and remittances to their home villages.

9.name: Les Disciples de Najaf
9.text:
The Disciples of Najaf are a handful of young Lebanese Shia in Port-au-Prince who receive letters and pamphlets from relatives studying in the Iraqi seminaries, where the exiled Iranian Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini has taught since 1965. They meet in private and have no cleric of their own.

They reject their elders' caution and preach that the learned clergy must lead the oppressed against tyrants, imperialism and Zionism, seeing in Duvalier's terror a mirror of the Shah's. Without institutions or numbers, their only assets are conviction and a thin line of correspondence to Najaf and Lebanon.

10.name: La Maison de la Daawa
10.text:
The House of the Call is a prayer room kept by a few Palestinian and Syrian Sunni traders and a handful of Haitian converts in Port-au-Prince, supplied with Korans and French-language tracts by the Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962. Its members cherish the tradition that Dutty Boukman, who lit the slave revolt of 1791, was a Muslim.

The group is quietist and loyal to authority, preaching strict monotheism, prayer and personal morality, and avoiding any conflict with the regime. It is anti-communist and looks to King Faisal's Saudi Arabia for guidance and funds. Its leverage is confined to charity, scholarships and trade.

11.name: Les Veilleurs du Califat
11.text:
The Watchmen of the Caliphate are a few Haitian students and converts who met activists of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953, at universities in Paris and Brussels. At home and in the diaspora they circulate its tracts in French among students of the State University.

They reject nations, constitutions and both Cold War blocs, and preach the restoration of a single caliphate to unite the Muslim world and liberate the oppressed, presenting it as the answer to colonialism and dictatorship. Without members or money, their influence reaches only a few searching students.

12.name: La Fraternité de la Oumma
12.text:
The Fraternity of the Ummah is a study circle of Haitian students and Levantine youth who discovered the writings of Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb through the Muslim Brotherhood's exile network in Geneva and Paris around Said Ramadan. They meet for lessons, charity and debates about Islam's place in a Black republic.

They advocate gradual Islamic renewal through education, social welfare and moral discipline, condemn both atheist communism and the cruelty of the Duvalier state, and present Islam as a faith of liberation for the descendants of enslaved Africans. Their reach is a few dozen people in Port-au-Prince.

13.name: Parti de l'Unité Nationale
13.text:
The National Unity Party is the political machine of François Duvalier, elected president in 1957 and proclaimed President for Life in 1964. It is the only party permitted in Haiti, filling the legislature, ministries and prefectures with loyalists, while real power rests with the president, his family and the Tonton Macoutes. Duvalier is ailing, and the question of succession hangs over the regime.

Duvalierism blends noiriste nationalism, the cult of Papa Doc, patronage and terror. It claims to speak for the Black middle class and peasantry against the mulatto elite, plays Washington through its anti-communism while keeping its distance, and controls every lever of the state.

14.name: Église catholique en Haïti
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Haiti emerged scarred from Duvalier's conflict with Rome in the early 1960s, when foreign bishops, Jesuits and many priests were expelled and the president was excommunicated. The 1966 settlement with the Vatican gave Haiti its first native hierarchy, headed by Archbishop François-Wolff Ligondé of Port-au-Prince, and lifted the excommunication.

The hierarchy now coexists with the regime, preaching order, family and faith while competing with Vodou and expanding Protestant missions. It runs much of the country's education and charity. Its leverage lies in schools, parishes and moral authority among the bourgeoisie and the rural poor, and in a younger clergy uneasy with silence.

15.name: Les Grandes Familles
15.text:
The Great Families are the mulatto and Levantine merchant dynasties who control Haiti's import and export trade, coffee and sisal exports, and the banks and shops of the Port-au-Prince business district. Duvalier rose by attacking their privileges, yet most have reached an accommodation, paying voluntary contributions and partnering with regime figures in monopolies.

They want stability, low taxes, foreign credit and the return of the US aid suspended in 1963. They fear both peasant revolt and arbitrary Macoute extortion. Their leverage lies in money, foreign connections and the ability to move capital to Miami and New York.

16.name: Les Industriels de l'Assemblage
16.text:
The Assembly Industrialists are businessmen and engineers in Port-au-Prince who have begun setting up workshops stitching baseballs, garments and electronic parts for American firms, drawn by low wages and proximity to the United States. They find an ear among younger technocrats around the palace.

They call for free-trade zones, tax holidays, an end to state and Macoute monopolies, protection of foreign investment and a market economy open to the United States. Pro-American and impatient with the old merchant elite's privileges, they see Haiti's future as an industrial export platform. Their leverage lies in jobs and investor confidence.

17.name: Les Gardiens de la Forêt des Pins
17.native_full: Les Gardiens de la Forêt des Pins
17.text:
The Guardians of the Pine Forest are agronomists, foresters and teachers, many trained at the Damien agricultural school, who watch with alarm as charcoal burning and hillside farming strip Haiti's mountains. They take their name from the Forêt des Pins reserve in the southeast, one of the last large forests in the country.

They campaign for reforestation, soil conservation, protection of watersheds and sustainable peasant agriculture, warning that erosion threatens the nation's survival. Politically cautious, they work through ministries, foreign aid missions and rural parishes. Their leverage lies in expertise and the mounting evidence of ecological crisis.

18.name: Mouvement Ouvrier Paysan
18.text:
The Worker-Peasant Movement was founded in 1946 by the teacher and trade unionist Daniel Fignolé, idol of the Port-au-Prince poor, who was briefly provisional president in 1957 before being deported by the army. Fignolé lives in exile in New York, and the MOP survives through veteran militants and union memories in the capital's slums.

The MOP preaches the emancipation of the Black working masses and peasants, labour rights, fair wages and land, without Marxist doctrine or bloc alignment. Its strength was the rouleau compresseur, the steamroller of mass demonstrations in the capital. Its leverage lies in a still-loyal urban following and Fignolé's symbolic name.

19.name: Les Partisans de Cazale
19.text:
The Partisans of Cazale are young Haitian Marxists at home and in exile in Paris, Montreal and Santo Domingo who drew radical conclusions from the massacre of the peasants of Cazale in 1969, punished for sheltering communist fighters. Critical of the Moscow-aligned leadership, they read Mao and study the Cuban and Vietnamese experiences.

They argue for a protracted people's war rooted in the peasantry, rejecting both Soviet caution and urban conspiracy, and preach national liberation from American domination and the Duvalier state alike. Their base is students and exiled intellectuals. Their leverage lies in ideological energy and their bonds with peasant communities.

20.name: Les Griots
20.text:
The Griots are the noiriste intellectual school founded in the 1930s around the review of the same name by Lorimer Denis and the young physician François Duvalier, building on Jean Price-Mars's ethnological work. Their ideas, exalting the African roots of the Haitian people, became the doctrine of the regime after 1957.

They hold that the Black majority must rule through its own authentic leaders against the mulatto elite, celebrate Vodou as national heritage and reject Western cultural tutelage. Their audience is the Black middle class, teachers, functionaries and regime writers. Their leverage lies in supplying the ideological justification for Duvalier's power.

21.name: Volontaires de la Sécurité Nationale
21.text:
The Volunteers for National Security, known everywhere as the Tonton Macoutes, are the paramilitary militia Duvalier organized from 1959 to counter the army. Tens of thousands strong, they are commanded by Rosalie Adolphe, known as Madame Max Adolphe, and answer to the president alone; figures such as Luckner Cambronne have grown rich in their shadow.

The Macoutes enforce Duvalierism through terror, extortion, murder and denunciation, blending noiriste ideology, Vodou symbolism and absolute loyalty to the chief. Recruited from the urban poor, rural section chiefs and the Black middle class, they control villages, markets and roadblocks. Their leverage is fear itself.

22.name: Forces Armées d'Haïti
22.text:
The Armed Forces of Haiti, created during the American occupation of 1915–1934 as the Garde d'Haïti, made and unmade presidents until Duvalier broke their power. Repeated purges, executions of officers and the rise of the Tonton Macoutes and the Presidential Guard have reduced the army to a subordinate force, poorly equipped and closely watched.

The officer corps remains anti-communist and US-trained, resentful of the militia and mindful of its old role as arbiter of politics. Officers in exile plot with Dominican and American contacts. Its leverage lies in its weapons, its coastal and provincial garrisons and the succession crisis that Duvalier's illness makes imminent.

23.name: La Cour de Sans-Souci
23.text:
The Court of Sans-Souci is a circle of northern notables, historians and descendants of the nobility of the Kingdom of Haiti who cherish the memory of King Henri Christophe, whose palace of Sans-Souci and Citadelle Laferrière dominate the hills above Milot. Others recall Emperor Faustin Soulouque's empire of 1849–1859.

They celebrate Haiti's Black monarchs as proof of national grandeur and argue for a strong hereditary authority above parties, discipline, public works and pride in the north. They lack a pretender and any political organization. Their influence lies in the cultural societies of Cap-Haïtien and in Haitian historical memory.
